input_format: citation. retrieval_title. retrieval_summary. authority_class. legal_regime. raw_text

scenarios.query: We're about to run a facilities management procurement worth around £195,000 for the council. How do we work out whether this contract has to go through the full procurement process, or whether it counts as below the relevant threshold for a body like ours?

We've decided who's won our tender and want to sign the contract quickly, but a losing bidder is unhappy. How long do we legally have to wait after telling the market about the award decision before we can actually sign the contract?

We published a full tender competition for this contract but the only response we got doesn't meet our requirements and would fail evaluation anyway. Can we just go and agree a contract with a supplier we already trust instead of running the competition again, and is there anything we have to publish first if we do that?

Before we finalise the tender pack, can we insist bidders already have the contract-specific insurance in place before we award, and can we require audited accounts from every single bidder, even the very small ones?

Our capital programme arrangement needs to run well beyond the usual term cap on these agreements - is there a route that lets us keep something like this going for a decade, and if so what does setting it up that way actually require us to build in from the start?

Once we've got a solid working group of suppliers on our staffing list, can we just close it to new joiners for a while to cut down on admin, or are we required to keep taking new applications the whole time the arrangement runs?

If a supplier becomes caught up in something that would normally have kept them out of the running, but this only comes to light after the contract has already started, can we pull the plug on the deal now, and what do we have to do before and after we do?

If costs on a live contract rise for reasons nobody could have seen coming, how far can we adjust the price with our existing supplier before that change becomes big enough that we would be required to go back out to competition instead?
Are we allowed to add this extra building to the existing contract without starting a fresh procurement, and is there anything we have to publish before we make the change?
Are we allowed to talk to suppliers like this before we go out to tender, what do we need to do to keep it fair to everyone, and is there anything we need to publish about it?
Is there a legal deadline by which we must pay this supplier's invoices, and do we have any separate obligation to report on how well we're paying on time?
Do we actually have to consider splitting this into separate area-based contracts, and if we do go with separate lots, can we limit how many a single bidder is allowed to win?

We ran our competition and awarded this contract under the old procurement regulations, just before the new Procurement Act rules came into force. We now want to use an options clause from our original tender documents to instruct some extra resurfacing works. Does a live contract like this automatically move onto the new Act's rules for making changes now that the Act is in force, or does something else determine which rulebook we follow?

We're about to award a call-off contract to one of our framework suppliers after running a mini-competition between them. Do we have to observe the same mandatory standstill period before we sign that we would for a contract awarded through a full open tender, or does the position differ for call-off contracts under a framework?

We want to talk to potential suppliers before we go out to tender, to understand what's available and help us write a realistic specification, but we're worried this could be seen as favouring our existing supplier or distorting the eventual competition. What do we actually need to do to run this safely?

Before we go out to tender for our combined estates services contract across several campuses, do we need to consider splitting the requirement into lots, and what do we need to record if we decide to keep it as a single contract?

We've had an FOI request for a supplier's pricing information from a contract we just awarded, and the supplier says it's commercially sensitive. Is there an actual legal exemption that lets us withhold it, and what's the real test that applies, not just what the supplier assumes because they marked it confidential?

Before we let a bidder move on to the next stage of our procurement, is there an actual legal requirement to check whether they should be excluded, or is that just recommended good practice? I want to know what the law itself requires, not a training summary.

We invited tenders for a highways contract but every bid we got back was rejected as unsuitable. Can we now just award the contract directly to one of those bidders without starting a new competition, and what do we need to check or publish before doing that?

We published our tender notice for this contract back in January 2025, before the procurement rules changed, but we're only going to finish the competition and award the contract now. Which set of rules do we need to follow to finish this off - the ones that were in force when we started, or the current ones?

Given the framework we're calling off from already has its own performance regime built in, do we still need to separately set our own key performance indicators on this individual piece of work, or does the framework-level arrangement already cover that requirement for us?

When comparing tenders on things like price and quality, is there a legal requirement about how we go about deciding who wins, and do we have to tell people publicly who we've picked before the contract is actually signed?

Someone outside the organisation has asked to see detailed pricing from one of our live supplier contracts, and the supplier objects to it being released. What are the grounds, if any, for keeping that information back, and what would we need to be able to show to rely on them rather than just asserting it?

Can we bring a new supplier into the later round of our procedure given how weak the field was, and separately, what do we need to do before we can exclude a bidder over a problem linked to its proposed sub-contractor?

We ran a competitive tender for a specialist technical service, and neither of the two bids we got met our minimum quality bar, so neither could be taken forward. We still need this work done and don't want to just walk away from the requirement. Can we move to negotiating and awarding the contract directly to one of the bidders instead of starting the whole competition again, and if so, what do we need to do first?

We run a framework for recurring minor works and want a structure that lets us periodically reopen it to new suppliers over several years instead of closing it after one round. What are the practical rules for how often we have to reopen it, how long each round can last, and what happens to the suppliers already on it when we do?

Partway through our highways contract, a survey has revealed contamination requiring significantly more remedial work than we originally scoped, and the contract didn't anticipate this. Can we instruct our existing contractor to do the extra work without running a new procurement, and is there a limit on how much extra value we can add this way?

We're looking at increasing the price on one of our contracts by around 12% and adding a new support tier, and we'd rather not run a whole new procurement for that. The contract was awarded a while back, before the procurement rules changed -- does that affect which modification rules apply, and would a change like this be allowed without a new competition?
Does the pipeline notice cover direct awards and routes to market via a framework? And, presumably, under Section 93 notices, 'contracts' would include Frameworks/DPS?
Will all values stated in the new regulations be inclusive of VAT, so that any trigger value is calculated on the same basis?
How formal does preliminary market engagement need to be to trigger publication of the preliminary market engagement notice?
Could you be challenged if you do preliminary market engagement with a closed group of suppliers and do not open the opportunity up to anyone?
Can a planned procurement notice be used like a PIN as a call for competition?
Where does calling off a framework sit as one of the procedures, both under the existing regulations and the new Act?
Will we be able to use the flexible framework regime for existing frameworks?
Are the Direct Award Justifications in Schedule 5 of the Act specifically aimed at direct awards of contracts, or can they also be applied to direct awards under a framework?
Can the objective mechanism for supplier selection in a framework simply state that the contract can be awarded directly to any framework provider?
Does the four-year framework length apply if you have a framework with lots but only one supplier per lot?
Must you have a second refresh or third framework, or could you re-open in year 3 and run the second framework to the end of the eight years?
Do contracts awarded under a framework need to run for the same duration as the framework, or can they run beyond it?
Will carry-over suppliers need to do any work to remain on a framework's subsequent stage, such as answering fresh questionnaires or submitting fresh documents?
What about the pre-selection thresholds for works and using standard selection? Also, what is the situation with regards PAS91 and CAS?
Can you still require suppliers to have delivered a comparable contract as a condition of participation, without requiring them to have worked with a particular authority?
What is the process for challenging the issue of a contract performance notice, and what liability or risks are there to a contracting authority if it is challenged?
Is it possible to reserve additional marks in an ITT evaluation stage for shortlisted suppliers only if this is clearly outlined in the tender instructions?
Is it possible to negotiate the price or any other aspects of the bid with the top-scoring bidder?
Is there guidance on whether the standstill period begins after the Contract Award Notice is published or when assessment summaries are sent to bidders?
Now that market engagement is explicitly covered in the Procurement Act, would market engagement activity be more directly subject to challenge?

For contracts valued over £5 million, unsuccessful supplier names will be published in the Contract Award Notice as well as successful supplier names. Is this related to the works threshold, or does it apply to goods and services too?
If a standstill period is extended because of a threatened challenge, will automatic suspension still be available throughout the extended period?
Will award letters still not need to be sent where a contracting authority awards a contract under a framework agreement or a dynamic purchasing system?
Are the positions on whether the 50% value cap for permitted modifications is cumulative under PCR 2015 contradictory?
If a modification increases the value of a contract to over £5 million, do you need to start publishing Contract Details Notices, Contract Performance Notices and copies of the modified contract?
Is there anything to prevent a contract being changed repeatedly without a Contract Change Notice if each individual change is within the permitted de minimis limit?
Section 75 does not apply to Light Touch Regime contracts even when above threshold. Is that also true of section 74?
We entered into the contract last week - do we need to publish an award notice?
It was an under-threshold contract and we didn't choose to advertise it on Contracts Finder but simply sought three quotes. Do we still need to publish contract award details on Contracts Finder?
What amounts to a substantial modification under Regulation 72?
What are the implied termination rights under Regulation 73?
Do I need to publish the advert anywhere else other than on the Find A Tender service?
Can I amend a Find A Tender service notice once it is published?
Our framework agreement has only six months left to run - can we call-off a two year specific contract?
Do we have to use the Cabinet Office SQ?
What criteria can we use at SQ stage?
What contract award procedures are available?
What is the innovation partnership process?
What information should be included in award letters/letters to unsuccessful bidders?
We sent out our award notification letters and today we have received a request from one of the unsuccessful bidders for a debrief - do we have to agree to this?
Do we need to answer bidder questions about the process during the standstill period?
A bidder has submitted a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request during the standstill period. Do we need to respond to the FOIA request before we can enter into the contract?
Does the fact that we have received a Freedom of Information Act request mean we have to disclose absolutely everything the bidder asks for?
We published a few award criteria and their percentage weightings in the contract documents. We now want to add more detail. Is there any problem with this approach?
If one of the prices from a bidder appears to be abnormally low, can we reject it without taking further action?
Before the end of the standstill period, an unsuccessful bidder puts us on notice that it has issued court proceedings. Can we award the contract anyway?
What are the time limits for an unsuccessful bidder to bring a claim?

Most PPNs only apply to procurements conducted under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015. Why does this PPN also apply to procurements conducted under the Utilities Contracts Regulations 2016, the Defence and Security Public Contracts Regulations 2011, and the Concessions Contracts Regulations 2016?

We're an executive agency running a below-threshold procurement for grounds maintenance. Can we limit the competition to businesses based in our county, and does the answer change depending on whether the procurement started before or after the Procurement Act 2023 came in?

Our department handles a lot of contractor-generated data under HMG contracts. Which government policy governs how that information should be classified, when was it last updated, and who does it apply to?

We're setting the award criteria for a £2m facilities management contract under the Procurement Act 2023 and want to include a social value criterion rewarding local job creation. What does that criterion legally need to satisfy, and how should we actually word and score it in practice?

We've awarded a £6m facilities contract under the Procurement Act 2023 with a subcontract worth over £1m attached to it. What are we legally required to build into the sub-contract on payment terms, and how are we now expected to actually check the prime is honouring that down the chain?

A supplier from a WTO Government Procurement Agreement country is worried that if it loses out on one of our contracts, it will only get whatever review process our domestic courts happen to offer. Is there an internationally guaranteed minimum standard of review it's entitled to, and does the UK's normal court-based challenge route actually satisfy it?

We are about to sign a £6.2 million grounds-maintenance contract. I know we need to set KPIs, but how do we decide which ones actually go in the contract details notice, and what happens to them once the contract is running?

A tenderer disclosed a past environmental prosecution that would normally trigger a discretionary exclusion ground. They say they've since cleaned up their act. What do we legally have to do before deciding whether to exclude them, and how do we actually judge whether their self-cleaning is good enough?

A shortlisted bidder shows up on the central government debarment list, but only under a discretionary exclusion ground, not a mandatory one. Are we still allowed to award to them, and what should we be doing before we make that call?

Our district council wants to call off a facilities-management contract under a framework that Crown Commercial Service set up, rather than run our own competition from scratch. Is that legitimate, and how do we satisfy ourselves it is?

We're two days into the standstill period for a £15m contract award, and a losing bidder has just told us it has filed a court claim challenging the decision. Are we now barred from signing, and what should we actually do about the standstill period we already published?

For a moderately complex services tender, what legal requirements do our award criteria have to meet, and what does the Act actually mean by an 'assessment methodology' that we need to publish alongside them?

We awarded a Public Contracts Regulations 2015 contract a couple of years ago, and the incumbent supplier has just agreed a fairly significant change to scope and price with us. If that change turns out to be a 'substantial modification' that should really have gone back out to tender, what termination rights does our contract need to have had in place for this, and what should we actually do now to close things out properly?

A genuine emergency has just landed on our desk - we need to put a contract in place fast under the old PCR2015 rules and there's no time to run a normal competition. Under what conditions could we actually justify awarding this without competing it at all, and what must we be doing on the paperwork side while we make that call?

We're about to tell bidders on a PCR2015-era competitive tender who's won, before we sign the contract. What has to be in that award decision notice, when are we actually allowed to sign afterwards, and what should our team be checking off before we send the notice out?

We're taking over management of a batch of low-value, low-risk contracts that were awarded some time ago. What's a proportionate way of running contract and supplier management for these day to day, from before-the-contract-starts through to renewal or exit, and does that change if we have to make a variation partway through?

We want to buy from an existing multi-supplier framework agreement rather than run a new competition from scratch. What should we be checking before we call off from it, can we re-apply our own selection criteria at that stage, and what does a mini-competition actually need to look like if the framework requires one?

We're managing a contract that was competitively tendered and awarded under the old Public Contracts Regulations, before the Procurement Act's rules came in. We still have to publish our annual prompt-payment statistics for it. Now that we're partway through this transition, do we keep reporting on the old financial-year basis, or does something change about how often we have to publish, and does the new Act's payment reporting regime apply to this contract instead?

We have an existing grounds-maintenance contract that we competitively tendered and awarded under the old procurement rules a couple of years ago, and at the time we told bidders we might come back for further similar work without running a new competition. We're now well past the Procurement Act's start date and want to place that follow-on order with the same contractor. Do we do that under the Act's own direct-award rules as if the original competition had never happened, or does something adjust how that justification works because the original contract was tendered under the old rules?

Our authority is running a defence-related procurement. We contacted a preferred bidder directly last year, before the Procurement Act's rules took effect, under the sole-source route available under the old defence and security procurement regulations, but we haven't signed anything yet. Now that the Act is fully in force, do we have to restart this using the new Act's rules, or can we finish it off under the regime we started it under?

We manage a multi-supplier framework agreement that was set up under the old Public Contracts Regulations before the Procurement Act took over, and it's still running its call-off competitions under those old rules. The UK has just signed new trade agreements with a couple of countries. Do suppliers based in those newly-covered countries now count as eligible international-trade-agreement suppliers for call-offs under our existing framework, or does that only start to matter for procurements run under the new Act?

We identified that only one supplier could realistically deliver a specialist repair part protected by their patent, so we formally approached them on that basis under the old procurement rules, without publishing anything, a little before the Procurement Act's rules took effect. We still haven't signed a contract with them. Does simply having contacted them like that before the change-over date lock this procurement into the old rules, or do we now have to run it under the Act instead?

One of our commercial team excluded a bidder from a provider selection regime process and then found out the bidder is challenging the decision. What do we now have to do, and within what deadline, to keep the centre informed?

AWE plc is helping us scope a defence-related contract. For the purposes of applying the Procurement Act's defence and security threshold, is AWE actually treated as a 'defence authority', or does that label only apply to the MOD itself?

We're a Scottish health board (a devolved Scottish authority) planning to run a framework jointly with an English NHS trust, using a UK-wide reserved procurement arrangement. I thought the Procurement Act doesn't apply to us as a devolved Scottish authority — does it apply here because we're procuring jointly with an English body?

Before we publish a contract details notice on a contract we're about to award, is there anything we're required to get from the winning supplier first about their central digital platform registration and their SME status?

We're partway through a procurement we started under the old rules before the Procurement Act commenced. We've just discovered the frontrunner bidder's UK subsidiary was convicted of a corruption offence four years ago. Do we have to exclude them, and for how long does that kind of exclusion normally last?

Our council wants to award a contract to a company we jointly control with two neighbouring councils, without running a competition, on the basis that it's really an in-house arrangement. This procurement started before the new Act came in — what's the actual legal test we need to meet?

Before launching a tender we started planning under the old regime, can we talk informally to a couple of specialist suppliers to help us write realistic specifications, without that being treated as unlawful favouritism later?
